rounds.text: Redington Ltd is trading at an attractive valuation with a price-to-earnings ratio of 13.6x [E1] and a market capitalization of ₹ 27,377 Cr [E3], backed by robust fundamentals including a return on capital employed of 18.4% [E12] and a return on equity of 16.9% [E13]. The business demonstrates powerful top-line and bottom-line momentum, highlighted by a trailing twelve-month compounded sales growth of 31% [E17] and a compounded profit growth of 47% [E21]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow model values the intrinsic worth at ₹ 710 per share compared to the market price of ₹ 350, providing a significant margin of safety of 50.7% [E44, E45], while a reverse DCF indicates that today's price prices in only 6.3% earnings growth against a base case expectation of 16.0% [E46]. Institutional confidence is expanding concurrently, with foreign institutional holding rising to 63.42% in September 2026 from 56.99% in December 2023 [E41], and rules-based screening scores the company at 88 out of 100 with a medium confidence buy signal [E60]. Conceded: cash conversion stands at a weak 0.18x for March 2026 where reported profits outpace operating cash flow [E34], and borrowings have increased to ₹ 6,364 Cr in September 2026 from ₹ 2,842 Cr a year prior [E39].

Redington’s financial health is undermined by a significant disconnect between reported profits and actual cash generation, evidenced by a concerning cash conversion ratio of just 0.18x as of March 2026 [E34]. This discrepancy suggests that the company’s earnings are heavily reliant on receivables or accruals rather than liquid inflows [E34]. Furthermore, the company has aggressively increased its debt load, with borrowings surging to Rs 6,364 Cr in September 2026 from Rs 2,842 Cr just one year prior [E39]. While the company maintains a moderate debt-to-equity ratio of 0.59x, this rapid accumulation of liabilities warrants caution [E37, E39]. Valuation metrics also signal potential overextension, as the EV/EBITDA ratio of 11.73x sits above the sector benchmark of 10.54x [E11]. Conceded: the company shows strong sales growth [E15, E17], high institutional interest [E41, E43], and a solid return on equity [E9, E13]. Despite these strengths, investors must weigh the risks of decelerating earnings growth [E65] and the historical volatility of the stock, which has experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of 80.2% [E52].

Conceded: cash conversion stands at 0.18x for March 2026 [E34]. However, this is more than offset by actual operational liquidity, as the company still generated positive operating cash flow of Rs 231 Cr and free cash flow of Rs 125 Cr in that same period [E35, E36]. Regarding borrowings surging to Rs 6,364 Cr [E39], this accompanies top-line expansion where compounded sales growth reached 31% in the trailing twelve months and profit growth hit 47% [E17, E21], while maintaining a manageable debt-to-equity ratio of 0.59x [E37]. While EV/EBITDA of 11.73x is slightly above the sector benchmark of 10.54x [E11], Redington compensates with superior capital efficiency, delivering an ROCE of 16.15% against the sector benchmark of just 6.96% [E10] and an ROE of 18.62% compared to the sector benchmark of 5.46% [E9]. Conceded: historical volatility includes a severe peak-to-trough drawdown [E52], yet institutional confidence remains high with foreign holding rising to 63.42% and positive institutional money flow [E41, E43].

While top-line expansion accompanied the borrowing surge, total borrowings more than doubled to Rs 6,364 Cr in September 2026 compared to Rs 2,842 Cr a year prior [E39]. However, domestic institutions simultaneously reduced their holdings to 16.01% [E42], showing clear divergence among sophisticated investors. While the bull cites absolute operating cash flow of Rs 231 Cr and free cash flow of Rs 125 Cr [E35, E36], it ignores the alarming cash conversion ratio of just 0.18x for March 2026, where reported profits drastically outpace actual cash generation and point to hidden risks in receivables and accruals [E34]. Conceded: the business shows an ROCE of 16.15% and ROE of 18.62% against lower sector benchmarks [E9, E10]. Yet this superior return profile is countered by a soaring debt load, with borrowings more than doubling to Rs 6,364 Cr in September 2026 from Rs 2,842 Cr a year prior [E39], alongside a thin current ratio buffer of 1.41x [E38]. Furthermore, dismissing the historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -80.2% as a relic ignores the very real danger posed by an annualized volatility of 42.7% [E52, E53]. Finally, the automated screen itself flags that earnings growth is actively decelerating, undermining the sustainability of the bull's growth narrative [E65].
